stem: A team tunes a support-bot prompt by eyeballing a handful of chats, and each fix seems to break some other case. What should they do first?

choices.text: Hand-grade ten ideal conversations in depth before every change
choices.reason: The guidance prioritizes volume: more automatically graded questions beat fewer high-quality hand-graded ones.

choices.text: Test only typical, well-formed customer messages
choices.reason: Evals should mirror the real task distribution, and the guidance says not to forget edge cases.

choices.text: Define success criteria, then build a task-specific eval set with edge cases and automated grading to score each prompt version
choices.reason: Correct: defining success criteria and designing evaluations to measure against them is the cycle central to prompt engineering.

choices.text: Keep rewording the prompt until the handful of chats look right
choices.reason: A few eyeballed chats don't mirror the real task distribution, so you can't tell whether a change helped overall.

takeaway: Measure, don't eyeball: set **success criteria**, then build an **automated, task-specific** eval set that includes edge cases.
mnemonic: Criteria first, then many automated tests.

source.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

stem: Your app on Claude Opus 5.5 retries failed requests. One request returns HTTP 200 with `stop_reason: "refusal"` and empty content. Your handler re-sends it unchanged to the same model, which refuses again. What's the better recovery?

choices.text: Keep retrying the same model with exponential backoff
choices.reason: A refusal is a normal response, not an error, and re-sending a refused request to the same model usually earns another refusal.

choices.text: Re-send it on a fallback model, or let server-side fallback (`fallbacks`) retry it
choices.reason: Correct: you can usually still get an answer by sending the same request to another Claude model; server-side fallback (beta) does this in one API call.

choices.text: Parse `stop_details.explanation` to decide whether to retry
choices.reason: The explanation text isn't stable, so display it rather than parse it; branch on `stop_reason` equal to `"refusal"`.

choices.text: Record it as a 5xx error so your error-rate alerts fire
choices.reason: A refusal is an HTTP 200, so monitoring built on error rates or 5xx never sees it. Instrument refusals as their own signal.

takeaway: A refusal is a **model-output** outcome, not a transient error: retry on a **different model**, not the same one.
mnemonic: Refused? Change the model, not the timing.

diagram.caption: Another Claude model can usually serve a refused request.

stem: After you move your agent to a newer Claude model, a tool handler that compares the tool input's raw JSON text with an expected string starts failing, even though the values look the same when printed. What should you change?

choices.text: Parse the input with `JSON.parse()` or `json.loads()` and compare the values
choices.reason: Correct: Unicode and forward-slash escaping differs between model versions (Opus 4.6+), so never do raw string matching on serialized input.

choices.text: Add `strict: true` to the tool definition
choices.reason: Strict mode is the fix for invented parameters and wrong parameter types, not for how the same values are escaped.

choices.text: Sharpen the tool's description
choices.reason: Sharper descriptions fix Claude calling the wrong tool; here the right tool is called with the right values.

choices.text: Add `input_examples` that show the exact expected string
choices.reason: `input_examples` help when Claude never calls a tool or picks values outside your enum; for escaping differences, the fix is to parse the JSON.

takeaway: Compare **parsed** tool inputs, never serialized strings: escaping can differ between model versions.

stem: You use Claude to grade 2,000 support replies for helpfulness. The grader writes paragraphs of free-form commentary that are hard to aggregate, and similar replies get different verdicts. Which change follows Anthropic's tips for LLM-based grading?

choices.text: Switch to human grading for all 2,000 replies
choices.reason: Human grading is the most flexible and high quality, but slow and expensive; the guidance says to avoid it if possible.

choices.text: Grade by exact match against one golden reply
choices.reason: Code-based grading is fast and reliable, but lacks nuance for complex judgments like helpfulness.

choices.text: Ask the grader for a score only, with no reasoning
choices.reason: The tips say to have the grader reason first, then discard the reasoning; this improves performance on tasks requiring complex judgment.

choices.text: Give a detailed rubric, and have it reason first, then output only "correct" or "incorrect" (or 1–5)
choices.reason: Correct: use detailed, clear rubrics and an empirical or specific output (purely qualitative evaluations are hard to assess at scale), with reasoning first.

takeaway: An LLM grader needs a **clear rubric**, a **specific output** and reasoning first; test its reliability before you scale.

source.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

stem: Your Agent SDK service exports OpenTelemetry traces. While debugging a bad run, you see spans with durations, model names and tool names, but nothing about what the tools returned. What explains this, and what should you change?

choices.text: Traces need `CLAUDE_CODE_ENHANCED_TELEMETRY_BETA=1`; set it
choices.reason: That variable is what enables traces, which you already have; it doesn't add tool content to them.

choices.text: Content isn't recorded by default; set `OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT=1` if your pipeline is approved to store it
choices.reason: Correct: telemetry is structural by default. `OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT=1` adds a `tool.output` span event with tool results, and requires tracing.

choices.text: Set the exporter to `console` to see the full output
choices.reason: Don't use `console` through the SDK: it writes telemetry to standard output, which the SDK uses as its message channel.

choices.text: Lower the export intervals so data isn't dropped
choices.reason: Shorter intervals reduce the chance of losing batched telemetry when a process exits; they don't add content to spans.

takeaway: Agent SDK telemetry records **structure**, not content, by default; turn content on only for pipelines approved to store it.

stem: Your tool-using agent with thinking worked until you changed the loop to drop `thinking` blocks from each assistant message before appending the `tool_result`, to save tokens. Now every follow-up request fails with 400 `invalid_request_error`, and SDK retries don't help. What's the cause?

choices.text: The API is overloaded; retry with a longer backoff
choices.reason: Overload is `529 overloaded_error`. A 400 means an issue with the format or content of your request, which a retry sends again unchanged.

choices.text: Your API key lacks access to thinking; rotate it
choices.reason: Key problems show up as `401 authentication_error` or `403 permission_error`, not as a 400 about your request.

choices.text: The model no longer supports thinking; switch to `thinking.type.enabled`
choices.reason: Sending `thinking.type.enabled` to Claude 4.7 and later models itself returns a 400, and your requests worked before the loop change.

choices.text: Your loop filtered out thinking blocks; pass every `thinking` and `redacted_thinking` block back exactly as received
choices.reason: Correct: thinking blocks in the latest assistant message that are edited, reordered, filtered out or reconstructed return a 400; pass them back unchanged.

takeaway: A 400 after a code change is an **integration** bug: fix what your request sends instead of retrying it.
